title: PSI in diff() drops the one-sided bins that matter most
body:
Ran into #1235 while comparing two profiled extracts and getting a suspiciously calm PSI back.

The repro there is exact: a categorical column where a brand-new category takes 25% of the population reports `psi` 0.069 from `diff()`, i.e. "no significant population change" by the thresholds in the docstring. The chi2 entry in the same diff reacts fine, so it's specifically the PSI path.

Two spots both skip exactly the bins that carry the biggest signal:

- `NumericStatsMixin._calculate_psi` computes `(other - self) * ln(other / self)` and then drops any term that comes out `inf` — which is what you get whenever a bin is zero on one side.
- `CategoricalColumn.diff` only sums a category when `percent_other != 0 and percent_self != 0`, so one-sided categories (preprocessed in with count 0 by `_preprocess_for_categorical_psi_calculation`) never contribute.

What I changed: both paths now go through a shared `profiler_utils.calculate_psi_term`, which substitutes a small epsilon (`PSI_ZERO_SHARE_EPSILON = 1e-4`) for a zero share before the log — the standard PSI practice the issue suggests. Bins that are zero on both sides still contribute nothing. The categorical assignment also moved out of the loop (it was being re-set every iteration, harmless but confusing), and `_calculate_psi`'s docstring now documents the zero-share handling.

On the issue's examples this takes the numeric case from 1.119 to ~3.87 and the categorical one from 0.069 to ~2.03 (reference values with eps=1e-4: 3.80 / 2.03 — the small delta on the numeric side is bin regeneration on random data, the categorical one lands on the reference when fed exact counts).

Worth being explicit about: this changes existing diff expectations. I verified each updated expectation by reproducing the old value with the skip semantics and the new value with an independent epsilon-PSI calculation, so the delta in each test is purely the one-sided bins now counting. Tiny-sample histograms (the float/int diff tests) can produce large PSI values now, which is honest — those distributions genuinely don't overlap — but reviewers should sanity-check that semantic.

Tests: the three touched profiler test files plus the float/int/compiler diff tests all pass locally (174 passed). `test_categorical_mapping` fails the same way on a clean checkout of main, looks unrelated (NaN null-index count).

Closes #1235

title: fix(labelers): count a predicted label with no support in the macro average
body:
Fixes #1229.

`evaluate_accuracy` rescales sklearn's macro average by `len(label_names) / labels with support`, to undo the zeros sklearn contributes for labels that never occur in the truth. The count that produces that denominator looked only at `support`, so a label that **never occurs in the truth but is still predicted** was dropped from it too. Every prediction of such a label is a false positive, so it has a measured precision of 0 — and dropping it both hid those false positives and inflated the rescale.

## Measured before the change

Running the function with the mapping `{0: PAD, 1: UNKNOWN, 2: ADDRESS, 3: SSN, 4: PERSON}` and the default `omitted_labels`, on ground truth of 100 `ADDRESS` characters plus 100 background characters:

| case | prediction | returned `f1` | macro P | micro P |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| control: perfect | — | 1.0000 | 1.0 | 1.0 |
| **100 background characters tagged `SSN`** | — | **1.0000** | **1.0** | 0.5 |
| **100 background characters split over `SSN` + `PERSON`** | — | **1.0000** | **1.0** | 0.5 |
| **40 of 100 `ADDRESS` characters tagged `SSN`** | — | 0.7500 | **1.0** | 0.6 |
| control: background tagged `ADDRESS` | — | 0.6667 | 0.5 | 0.5 |
| control: everything tagged `SSN` | — | 0.0000 | 0.0 | 0.0 |

A model that tags background text with an absent label scored a perfect `f1`, and mislabelling 40% of one label's characters did not move the precision component at all.

## Change

A label counts toward the average when it occurs in the truth (`support`) **or** when anything was predicted as it, which is its column of the confusion matrix being non-empty:

```python
label_index = label_index_by_name.get(key)
predicted_as_label = label_index is not None and bool(
    conf_mat[:, label_index].sum()
)
if values["support"] or predicted_as_label:
    num_labels_with_positive_support += 1
```

After it, the same cases return 0.5000, 0.3333 and 0.3750 — the average over the labels that the truth or the prediction actually used. The controls are untouched, and a label that neither side used is still excluded.

## Tests

Two cases added next to `test_no_support_classes`:

- `test_predicted_label_without_support_lowers_f1` — the false positive now costs half the returned `f1`, and the per-label row shows `precision 0` with `support 0`.
- `test_label_neither_predicted_nor_in_truth_is_still_excluded` — the rescale still ignores a label nobody used, which is what `test_no_support_classes` relies on.

All six cases in `TestEvaluateAccuracy` pass, and the four existing ones return exactly the values they did before. This environment cannot install TensorFlow, so I ran them through `unittest` with `labeler_utils`' module-level `import tensorflow` stubbed; nothing in `evaluate_accuracy` touches it. `black`, `isort` and `flake8` are clean on both files.

Credit for the analysis in #1229 — the code location, the measured table and the direction of the fix are all from that report.

title: fix: update popmon_dp_loader_example notebook for popmon 1.0+ API
body:
Fixes #1014

## What was broken

The `popmon_dp_loader_example.ipynb` notebook errored on cell 6 with a `ValidationError: 2 validation errors for Settings` when run against modern popmon (v1.0+):

```ValidationError: 2 validation errors for Settings
extended_report
Extra inputs are not permitted [type=extra_forbidden, ...]
pull_rules
Extra inputs are not permitted [type=extra_forbidden, ...]
```

## Root cause

popmon v1.0.0 migrated to a pydantic-based `Settings` model with `extra="forbid"`, which rejects the `extended_report` and `pull_rules` kwargs the notebook was passing directly to `pm_stability_report`.

## Changes

Migrated the three `pm_stability_report` calls to use a `Settings` object:

- `extended_report` → `settings.report.extended_report`
- `pull_rules` → renamed to `monitoring_rules` and moved to `settings.monitoring.monitoring_rules`
- `time_axis` → set on `settings.time_axis` (the kwarg is silently ignored when settings is provided)

Added a `make_settings(time_axis)` helper so each call gets a fresh `Settings` instance, since `settings.bin_specs` gets mutated per-call and can't be reused across calls.

## Testing

Verified the notebook executes end to end against popmon 1.4.12:

```
jupyter nbconvert --to notebook --execute popmon_dp_loader_example.ipynb --output /tmp/test.ipynb
[NbConvertApp] Writing 53035 bytes to /tmp/test.ipynb
```

All three `pm_stability_report` calls complete successfully and produce stability reports.

## Summary
Fixes #1147

## Problem
Pytest was generating collection warnings because helper classes named `TestColumn` and `TestColumnWProps` were being detected as test classes due to their 'Test' prefix, but failed collection because they have `__init__` constructors.

```
PytestCollectionWarning: cannot collect test class 'TestColumn' 
because it has a __init__ constructor
```

## Solution
Renamed the helper/mock classes:
- `TestColumn` → `MockColumn`
- `TestColumnWProps` → `MockColumnWProps`

This makes it clear these are mock/helper classes, not test classes, and eliminates the pytest collection warnings.

## Files Changed
- `dataprofiler/tests/profilers/test_histogram_utils.py`
- `dataprofiler/tests/profilers/test_numeric_stats_mixin_profile.py`

## Testing
This is a straightforward refactoring with no logic changes. All existing tests should pass.

## Improvements for Local Development Setup and Unit Test Structure
This PR focuses on resolving issues with local environment setup and unit test execution in the dataprofiler library. The changes ensure a more reliable setup process, eliminate dependency conflicts, and enhance the performance and maintainability of unit tests. It also involves fixing Pre-commit Hook Errors.

## Changes Introduced
### 1. Refactored Makefile

- Dependency Installation Order: Moved `requirements-ml.txt` earlier in the installation sequence to prevent conflicts with TensorFlow and shared dependencies like NumPy.

- Help Section: Added a help target to display all available Makefile commands with descriptions. This makes the development workflow more transparent and easier to understand for new and existing contributors.

title: Multiprocessing and Performance Improvements
body:
This is related to some of the discussion in #1098

In my testing, I have a single dataset.  I am running this in a Docker container.  I'm running with the following settings:

```
import sys
import json
import time
import dataprofiler as dp

filename = "myfile.parquet"

def profile_test(filename):
    data = dp.Data(filename)
    profile_options = dp.ProfilerOptions()
    
    profile_options.set({
        "structured_options.data_labeler.is_enabled": False,
        "unstructured_options.data_labeler.is_enabled": False,
        "structured_options.correlation.is_enabled": False,
        "structured_options.multiprocess.is_enabled": True,
        "structured_options.chi2_homogeneity.is_enabled": False,
        "structured_options.category.max_sample_size_to_check_stop_condition": 1,
        "structured_options.category.stop_condition_unique_value_ratio": 0.001,
        "structured_options.sampling_ratio": 0.3,
        "structured_options.null_replication_metrics.is_enabled": False
    })

    print(profile_options)

    profile = dp.Profiler(data, options=profile_options)

    human_readable_report = profile.report(report_options={"output_format":"pretty"})

    with open("reportfile.json", "w") as outfile:
        outfile.write(json.dumps(human_readable_report, indent=4))

start_time = time.time()
profile_test(filename)
end_time = time.time()

print("Profile runtime for "+filename, end_time-start_time, 'seconds')
```

When Data Profiler gets to the first `tqdm` loop and displays `Finding the Null values in the columns...` it's pretty quick.  It also lists 19 processes corresponding to the pool_size available in the Python multiprocessing pool.  This works fine.

Then when it gets to the second `tqdm` loop and displays `Calculating the statistics...` I noticed that it was only using 4 processes.  When I looked at what was running, I am only seeing a single core being used.  When I looked at the code, `profile_builder.py` has 4 hard-coded.  This doesn't seem right.  There's a utility function `profiler_utils.suggest_pool_size` that's not even used anywhere in the codebase as far as I can tell that returns the pool size.  So I swapped that out.  Now when I run, instead of 4 processes it shows 19 so that seems better.  At least we're not leaving potential performance on the table with hard-coding.  

However, I'm still seeing only a single core being used.  I also checked the CPU affinity after reading some [comments on Stackoverflow](https://stackoverflow.com/questions/15639779/why-does-multiprocessing-use-only-a-single-core-after-i-import-numpy).  It looks reasonable to me.

```
print(f"Affinity: {os.sched_getaffinity(os.getpid())}")
```

I'm going to try profiling a bit more and see if I can figure out where it's hanging.  It seems like it should be faster, particularly on a multi-core machine.  Calculating all the statistics and stuff *is* taxing but it seems like it should be faster.
